::: {#def-adjusted-p-value}
#### Adjusted p-value

For a multiple testing procedure that takes a level $c$
($\siglevel$ for an FWER procedure, $q$ for an FDR procedure),
the **adjusted p-value** $\tilde p_j$ of $H_j$ is the smallest level at which the procedure rejects $H_j$,
or $1$ if there is none:

$$\tilde p_j \eqdef \min \set{c \in [0, 1] : \text{the procedure at level } c \text{ rejects } H_j}.$$

If the rejection set only grows as the level grows, as it does for the procedures on this page,
the procedure at level $c$ rejects exactly the hypotheses with $\tilde p_j \le c$,
so a reader can apply any level to a list of adjusted p-values without redoing the procedure.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#exm-adjusted-p-value}
#### Adjusted p-values for the Khan genes

For the Bonferroni correction, $H_j$ is rejected at level $c$ exactly when $m p_j \le c$,
so $\tilde p_j = \min\set{1, m p_j}$.
For Holm's procedure and BH the adjusted p-values are

$$
\tilde p_{(i)}^{\text{Holm}} = \max_{k \le i} \min\set{1, (m - k + 1)\, p_{(k)}},
\qquad
\tilde p_{(i)}^{\text{BH}} = \min_{k \ge i} \min\set{1, \frac{m\, p_{(k)}}{k}}.
$$

R computes all three with `p.adjust()`.
For the first ten genes:

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-p-values
data.frame(
  gene = names(ten_genes),
  p_value = ten_genes,
  bonferroni = p.adjust(ten_genes, method = "bonferroni"),
  holm = p.adjust(ten_genes, method = "holm"),
  bh = p.adjust(ten_genes, method = "BH"),
  row.names = NULL
) |>
  dplyr::arrange(p_value) |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(p_value:bh, fmt_p)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Rejecting the hypotheses whose adjusted p-value is at most the level
reproduces the rejection sets of the functions defined above, on all 2308 genes:

```{r}
#| label: adjusted-p-values-check
#| code-fold: false
levels_to_check <- c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1)
sapply(levels_to_check, function(a) {
  c(
    bonferroni = all(
      (p.adjust(khan_p, "bonferroni") <= a) == bonferroni_reject(khan_p, a)
    ),
    holm = all((p.adjust(khan_p, "holm") <= a) == holm_reject(khan_p, a)),
    bh = all((p.adjust(khan_p, "BH") <= a) == bh_reject(khan_p, a))
  )
}) |>
  `colnames<-`(levels_to_check)
```

The check confirms that the formulas and functions agree on these data at these levels;
it is not a proof that they agree for every data set.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#rem-q-value}
#### q-values

The BH adjusted p-value of a hypothesis is the smallest FDR level $q$ at which BH rejects it.
Some authors call this a *q-value*.
@storey2002direct defines the q-value with the same meaning,
but estimates the fraction $m_0 / m$ of true null hypotheses from the p-values
and multiplies by the estimate, $\hat\pi_0$, which is usually below 1.
BH is the case $\hat\pi_0 = 1$, so Storey's q-values are smaller, and reject more, when many null hypotheses are false.
:::
